children: Brain co-founder Andrew Ng is pushing back sharply against renewed warnings that advanced artificial intelligence could threaten humanity, calling extinction scenarios "much more science fiction than science" as the technology industry becomes increasingly divided over how quickly AI development should proceed.
Ng, who also co-founded Coursera, said he had been "quite dismayed over the past two weeks" by the latest wave of warnings from AI researchers and executives.

"This wave of PR has kicked up again, for probably similar purposes," Ng said, suggesting that catastrophic AI concerns have previously been amplified partly to influence regulation and attract attention.
His comments follow warnings from former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon, who argued that companies racing toward superintelligent systems could create catastrophic risks.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have also called for stronger safeguards and a slower approach to frontier AI development.
Ng does not dismiss AI risks entirely.

He pointed specifically to cybersecurity threats and argued that companies should concentrate on "practical engineering problems," stronger testing and safeguards rather than hypothetical extinction scenarios.
Investor Steve Eisman has gone even further.
"I think this is all nonsense," Eisman said, arguing that AI companies may have commercial reasons for promoting stronger regulation.
"They realize that there are no moats around their business whatsoever, and they're trying to manufacture a crisis that will create regulation."
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also opposed a broad development slowdown, arguing that safety should be treated primarily as an engineering challenge.
The debate increasingly matters beyond safety policy.
Stricter regulation could raise development costs, slow model releases and potentially favor the largest companies that already have the resources to comply.
That helps explain Eisman's concern that regulation itself could strengthen competitive moats.
The opposite approach carries its own risks. Faster development could accelerate demand for Nvidia
chips, data centers and AI infrastructure, but major safety failures could trigger much harsher regulation later.
For investors, the key issue is no longer simply whether AI improves quickly. It is whether regulators and industry leaders allow that development to continue at today's pace.

title: Google Brain Co-Founder Pushes Back on AI Doom Warnings
